The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Shop pages slowed down for shoppers
Why, in plain words: The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, which left too few servers to answer shoppers quickly.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 8m 58s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop - confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #536 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Shop pages slowed down for shoppers
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 02:37 to 02:45:58 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 03:03:41 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 02:45:28 UTC
Ended by: Argus: raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop - confirmed, still in place

Summary
The service broke at 02:37 UTC and was back to normal at 02:45:58 UTC, 8 minutes 58 seconds later. What its alert watches went from 214 ms before it began to 1713 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, which left too few servers to answer shoppers quickly. What Argus did: raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #536, for a person to review and merge. Argus left automatic sync of io-shop off, to be turned back on once its repository says what should run (AI-3). io-shop's pages could slow down again in the same way if its autoscaler floor goes back to 3 replicas while the scale-down setting in its repository is still unchanged.

Impact
8m 58s - onset until back to normal
1.1% to 1.4% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
214 ms to 1004 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 1713 ms; the rule's line is 600 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
The production autoscaler settings for io-shop set the scale-down stabilization window to 0, so the controller acts on the lower CPU per replica that its own scale-up to 6 replicas produced, drops straight back to 3, and at that count CPU per replica climbs past its 70% target and requests queue, which drives response times up until it scales up again. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
Causal chain
symptom Shoppers had to wait much longer than usual for io-shop's slowest requests to finish, while the share of failed requests stayed within its normal variation.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p95 latency above threshold for 5m
    T5 02:45:46 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:37
why 1 io-shop had too few replicas serving it for the load it was under. When the Investigator read the rollout at 02:45:49 UTC, all 3 replicas were running a single revision.
  Evidence:
    T9 02:45:49 Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
    M1 02:45:58 Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for C1: confirmed, still in place
    T18 02:48:10 Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:45
    T19 02:48:10 Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
    T20 02:48:10 Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - raised io-shop's autoscaler floor from 3 replicas to 6 and the rule that fired stopped firing
  Ruled out:
    A deploy, release or flag change on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:38; the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes. A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:45:52.
      T7
      T8
      T14
why 2 The autoscaler likely dropped back to its floor of 3 replicas right after each scale-up, since the production values file sets its scale-down stabilization window to 0.
  Evidence:
    F1 What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
Contributing factors
- No check was seen that would stop an autoscaler setting with a zero scale-down stabilization window from reaching production. (AI-4)
- No alert on the autoscaler moving io-shop's replica count back and forth was seen. The fault was found only by the latency alert. (AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | The autoscaler would not settle: cpu_limit_cores alternated between 3.0 and 6.0 from 02:33 UTC. p95 latency was high in the minutes served at 3 cores (02:37 UTC, 02:40 UTC, 02:41 UTC, 02:43 UTC) and back to baseline at 6 cores (02:39 UTC, 02:42 UTC). Traffic was ramping at the same time, but the capacity flapping is what separates the slow minutes from the normal ones. | 0.70 | confirmed
C2 | Demand grew from 1200 to 5400 requests per minute, which is 4.5 times the baseline, and the deployment's capacity was outgrown. The queueing shows up as latency at the 3-core limit. | 0.25 | confirmed, as tested for C1

Trigger
C1 was confirmed; it blames io-shop itself and names no change to it.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 02:45:58 | Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for C1 | Argus | can be put back | confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
 | 02:50:05 | Proposed a fix: PR #536 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 02:37 UTC. HighLatency fired at 02:45:03 UTC, 8 minutes 3 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p95 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #536 | open
AI-3 | Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand | mitigate | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Add a CI policy check that fails any service's deploy values whose autoscaler scale-down stabilization window is missing or set too low, so the check covers every change like this one and not only io-shop's own test. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Add an alert for when io-shop's autoscaler keeps moving the replica count up and down over a short stretch. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came 7 minutes 3 seconds after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
- 48 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent formed 2 candidate causes, best first: C1, C2.
- 49 seconds after the alert was raised, Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:45:52.
- 55 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for C1.
- 3 minutes 7 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 5 minutes 2 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #536.
What went wrong
- Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Response effort
none - engineer time
160,783 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/e76fe280-ebff-4192-9a9e-662bc475a73a
The fix it proposed: PR #536 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/536) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
G46bc | ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 23 occurrences in 14 minutes, 02:31–02:44
Gbac1 | WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 13 occurrences in 14 minutes, 02:31–02:44; # was 0.50% to 2.50%, typically 1.50%, highest at 02:37
Gad41 | INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 1 occurrence in 1 minute, 02:38
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | deploy/values-production.yaml renders the HorizontalPodAutoscaler with minReplicas 3, maxReplicas 6 and scaleDownStabilizationSeconds: 0. The file's own comment says what that window is for: the controller acts on a CPU reading that its last scaling action produced. With the window at 0, a scale-up to 6 lowers per-replica CPU. The next reading then looks like load has fallen, so the controller drops straight back to 3, CPU per replica climbs past the 70% target, and it scales up again. That loop matches the 3/6 alternation the investigation saw, with p95 high in the minutes at 3.

The change sets scaleDownStabilizationSeconds back to 300, the Kubernetes default the file's comment describes. The controller then acts on the highest recommendation from the last five minutes before scaling down, so it holds 6 replicas while traffic ramps instead of dropping back. Scale-up is unchanged and min/max are untouched.

The new test, tests/io_shop/test_deploy_values.py, reads the deployment file as plain text so it needs no YAML library. It fails if the scale-down stabilization window is missing or below 60 seconds, which catches this setting coming back as 0. Nothing in src/ reads the autoscaling block (a repository search finds no other reference), so no service code changes.
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist
✓ Key incident data collected (met)
✓ Impact assessed (met)
○ Root-cause analysis complete (for a person)
  running the proposed fix's tests against the current code would confirm the reading, not that the code it reads is what ran (AI-2)
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, the io-shop online shop's pages loaded slowly for some shoppers. The likely cause was the shop's automatic scaling repeatedly removing the extra servers it had just added, which left too few servers to answer shoppers quickly. Argus estimates the cost to the shop in takings at {customer_loss}. No one was paged, because no on-call incident was linked to this one. Argus ended the problem by raising the minimum number of servers the automatic scaling must keep running. Argus confirmed the change, and it is still in place, with automatic syncing left switched off. Argus has also proposed a fix, which is open as a draft and has not been applied.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
